pages/1/01.s: Ask precise questions, judge evidence, test assumptions, correct mistakes, and build understanding through practice.

pages/1/02.t: How a Computer Runs a Game
pages/1/02.s: Build a game from CPU instructions, a small program, stored values, and the services that make it interactive.

pages/1/03.s: Follow actions through a game's entities, checks, space, and time; distinguish live state, display copies, server decisions, saves, and bytes.

pages/1/04.s: Build a small Rust rule and use it to understand variables, logic, test cases, collections, and ways to organize code.

pages/1/05.s: Express programming logic in Rust: name state, choose a path, repeat work, group values, borrow safely, and handle missing or failed results.

pages/1/06.s: Turn observed game behavior into repeatable experiments, test a small tool, and record the evidence needed to reproduce its results.

pages/1/07.t: A Windows Lab You Can Reset
pages/1/07.s: Set up a Windows virtual machine with the compiler, debugger, memory scanner, course code, and recovery snapshots.

pages/1/08.s: Trace one game value through bytes, types, addresses, pointers, and offsets, then see why a found address can change.

pages/1/09.t: What a Memory Scan Really Finds
pages/1/09.s: Find, test, and change one gold value in Wesnoth, and see what each scan does and does not prove.

pages/1/17.s: Read a byte by its bit positions, select flags with masks, and distinguish discarded shift bits from wrapped rotation bits.

pages/1/13.t: Rust: Missing Values, Failures, and States
pages/1/13.s: Follow Option and Result through closures, early returns, and pattern matching, then represent game states with enums.

pages/1/14.s: Read iterator chains, overlapping windows, complete records, explicit byte conversion, integer limits, and C layout.

pages/1/15.t: Rust: Borrowed Views and Useful Interfaces
pages/1/15.s: Connect lifetimes, typed offsets, From and Into, Display, derived traits, generic capabilities, and validated builders.

pages/1/16.s: Use scope-bound cleanup, Drop, structured library errors, and application context without hiding failures.

pages/2/01.s: Learn what a debugger actually does and why pausing one instruction can answer a big question.

pages/1/10.t: How Source Becomes a Running Process
pages/1/10.s: Compare native compilation, bytecode interpretation, REPLs, and type checking; then follow a native program through linking and loading.

pages/2/02.t: How Assembly Describes a Running Game
pages/2/02.s: Understand what assembly is, how the CPU executes it, and how registers, memory, flags, stacks, and calls fit together.

pages/2/03.t: Breakpoints: One Moment of Program State
pages/2/03.s: Pause on an instruction or memory access, inspect registers, memory, and the call stack, and continue without losing the thread.

pages/2/04.t: From a Game Value to the Code That Changes It
pages/2/04.s: Follow a known gold address backward to the exact instruction that changes it.

pages/2/05.t: Tracing an Action Through Its Callers
pages/2/05.s: Follow callers and dependencies from one gold-changing instruction to the menu decision that caused it.

pages/2/08.s: Understand dynamic allocation, module bases, ASLR, and why a pointer path survives when one raw address does not.

pages/2/09.s: Trace the player object back to a verified starting point and prove the pointer path across restarts.

pages/2/06.s: Understand how a small detour can run extra instructions and still return the game to its original path.

pages/2/07.t: What a Working Detour Must Preserve
pages/2/07.s: Build a temporary debugger-only detour, prove every hop, and restore the target.

pages/2/10.t: Instruction Reference: Values and Integer Arithmetic
pages/2/10.s: Look up common x86 value operations, then explore each one with a worked trace.

pages/2/11.t: Instruction Reference: Decisions, Stack, and Bits
pages/2/11.s: Explore comparisons, branches, call stacks, masks, shifts, and debugger stops one instruction at a time.

pages/2/12.s: Trace speed, position, numeric conversions, and NaN comparisons using the SSE instructions common in game code.

pages/3/01.s: Learn the ownership, address, byte-buffer, error, and operating-system boundaries used by every memory tool.

pages/3/09.t: How Bytes Become Numbers and Pointers
pages/3/09.s: Work out by hand how whole numbers, negative numbers, and f32 floats are stored, and exactly what a pointer's type controls.

pages/3/02.t: How External Tools Read Game Memory
pages/3/02.s: Open the target, read a verified address, and write through a small checked process-memory wrapper.

pages/3/03.t: How C++ Objects Appear in Memory
pages/3/03.s: Turn repeated reads, member-function calls, and virtual dispatch into a tested object layout, then inspect it through typed snapshots.

pages/3/04.s: Recognize the shapes that factories, states, observers, singletons, and component systems leave in compiled code: repeated pointers, virtual calls, constructors, and update loops.

pages/3/05.t: How Collections Live and Die in Memory
pages/3/05.s: Identify vectors, strings, handles, component pools, reference counts, and destruction paths without assuming one compiler's private layout.

pages/3/06.s: Learn the difference between representation and security, trace small encode/decode paths, and implement a reversible value plus integrity check.

pages/3/07.t: How Text Becomes Bytes in a Game
pages/3/07.s: Trace visible text to bytes, understand encodings and terminators, and build checked strings at FFI boundaries.

pages/1/11.t: Game Engines: Where the Rules Live
pages/1/11.s: Separate the reusable engine from the game built on it, follow one frame and the clocks that drive it, the entities and the scenes inside it, see which engine each course game uses, and learn why where a rule lives decides how you change it.

pages/4/12.t: How an Engine Orders and Shares Its Work
pages/4/12.s: See how an engine's systems share data through components, resources, and events, how one frame's work is ordered and run in parallel, and how the engine notices only what changed.

pages/4/01.t: From One Player to a Game-State Snapshot
pages/4/01.s: See how one verified player layout becomes a bounded, typed snapshot of every side in a local match.

pages/4/02.s: Learn why live reads go stale and how snapshots, separate observation, and verified writes protect a game-state tool.

pages/4/03.t: Maps as Grids of Game State
pages/4/03.s: Understand a map as indexed game state, then trace and visualize one tile's visibility in an offline lab.

pages/4/04.s: Use a recruitment loop to see why feedback, named states, confirmation, and a safe stop make automation reliable.

pages/4/11.s: Build distance and direction from positions, use normalization and dot products to express spatial decisions, then blend values and test contact with simple shapes.

pages/4/05.s: Trace player and enemy positions in offline Flare, then choose actions from validated coordinates rather than fixed timings.

pages/4/06.s: Turn a verified tile grid into routes with BFS or A-Star, keeping map observation separate from game input.

pages/4/07.t: When Changed State Becomes an Event
pages/4/07.s: Turn repeated polls into meaningful events with snapshot differences, debouncing, confirmation, and cooldowns.

pages/4/08.s: Record changing game state without delaying observation, hiding dropped samples, or losing the log's meaning.

pages/4/09.s: Follow a guard through sensing, delayed reactions, and state changes to understand how games choose an NPC's next action.

pages/4/10.t: How an NPC Sees, Chooses, and Remembers
pages/4/10.s: Work through the arithmetic inside Lesson 4.12's toy guard: Pythagoras and the dot product behind its view cone, stepped line-of-sight checks, utility scores and their switch points, behavior trees, and the byte offsets of its structure.

pages/7/01.s: Use the PE header and section map to understand where a Windows executable keeps code, data, imports, and addresses.

pages/7/02.t: File Offsets, RVAs, and Live Addresses
pages/7/02.s: Connect positions in a PE file to relative virtual addresses and the addresses Windows gives its loaded modules.

pages/7/03.s: Understand how a DLL publishes functions through data directories, names, ordinals, addresses, and forwarded exports.

pages/7/04.s: See how byte patterns locate candidate instructions across known builds, and why wildcards and semantic checks matter.

pages/7/05.s: Understand region permissions, copied snapshots, candidate filtering, and guarded writes in a value scanner.

pages/7/06.s: See how a disassembler finds boundaries and meanings in variable-length x86 byte streams.

pages/7/07.s: Understand how Windows debug events, breakpoint bytes, and thread state let a debugger pause and resume a real instruction.

pages/7/08.s: Connect scanning, decoding, breakpoints, and bounded logging to a trace of calls made by a running game.

pages/7/09.s: Understand how ETW records time-stamped events around a running game and how to read a short performance trace.

pages/8/05.s: Use immutable memory snapshots, bounded workers, cancellation, and sorted results to make scanning faster without losing reproducibility.

pages/3/08.t: What a DLL Function Promises Its Caller
pages/3/08.s: Infer an exported function's parameters, calling convention, result, and ownership rules before wrapping it in a small typed API.

pages/8/01.s: Understand what changes when Rust code runs inside a game process and how DLL loading constrains initialization.

pages/8/02.s: Follow the module path, process handle, remote memory, and loader call involved in loading a DLL into a controlled game process.

pages/8/03.s: Understand how a detour redirects execution, preserves displaced instructions, verifies target bytes, and restores the original path.

pages/8/04.s: See how an imported function pointer can be redirected inside a controlled process and safely restored.

pages/8/11.s: Follow a key press, a stick movement, and a mouse move from the device to a game action, and see why buttons have edges, sticks have dead zones, and typed text is not the same as keys.

pages/8/06.t: Windows Input: Polling, Events, and Messages
pages/8/06.s: Compare hotkey polling, synthetic input, and window messages so a local game tool chooses the right input boundary, and see how the window's client area, scale, and several windows change the coordinates it works with.

pages/8/07.t: Menus as State and Command Interfaces
pages/8/07.s: See how a settings menu expresses feature state, sends commands to a worker, and shuts down without leaving stale changes.

pages/8/10.s: Organize a local tool around owned snapshots, typed commands, feature lifecycles, version checks, and dependable cleanup.

pages/13/05.s: A hook changes live control flow under threads, ABI rules, and versioned bytes; safe installation and removal preserve those contracts.

pages/5/01.s: Follow a world-space point through engine axis conventions, camera axes, object transforms and their local and world copies, quaternions, homogeneous coordinates, perspective or orthographic projection, several cameras with their own viewports, and screen pixels and texture coordinates.

pages/5/02.t: The Rendering Pipeline and Its State
pages/5/02.s: See how objects become pixels through meshes, materials, light, shaders, rasterization, depth testing, transparency, visibility flags and layers, culling, render passes, HDR and anti-aliasing, the renderer's own copy of the world, and the 2D case, and the state that gives each draw its meaning.

pages/5/03.s: Understand what indexed OpenGL draws request, how bound state and shader inputs change their meaning, why many small draws cost frame time, and why observation must keep the render thread moving.

pages/5/04.s: Use temporary color to distinguish render categories while accounting for materials, lighting, blending, and color space.

pages/5/05.s: See how a camera ray, collision query, and occlusion test become a game's crosshair target, and how the same ray from a mouse cursor picks what is under it.

pages/5/06.s: Connect vectors to yaw, pitch, angular error, target ranking, how animation poses a skeleton, target points, timing, and projectile motion.

pages/5/07.s: Separate input, weapon kick, random spread, camera shake and other camera motion, and recovery to understand why the view moves after a shot.

pages/5/08.s: Follow entities through radar filtering, coordinate transforms, scale, clipping, and marker rules.

pages/5/09.s: Follow a 3D point through world, view, clip, normalized, and screen coordinates to place stable overlays.

pages/5/10.s: Understand how COM vtables expose Direct3D methods, why export lookup differs from OpenGL, and how a reversible swap-chain hook works.

pages/5/11.t: Direct3D Draw Calls and Bound State
pages/5/11.s: Read Direct3D draw calls in the context of their bound state and compare what the same arguments mean in Direct3D 9 and 11.

pages/8/08.s: Combine camera and player observations, graphics features, versioned profiles, and reversible hooks without mixing frames or losing game state.

pages/8/09.s: Understand what a game's interface is made of, how its text function can draw a small menu, and why input edges, frame timing, and string lifetimes matter.

pages/6/01.s: See how a client and server turn a move into framed bytes, and why TCP transport does not define a game's message boundaries.

pages/6/02.s: Learn how a short local capture reveals message direction, boundaries, and the bytes associated with one game action.

pages/6/03.s: Connect raw chat frames to typed messages through bounded parsing, serialization, and round-trip checks.

pages/6/04.s: Understand legal message order through session states, replay, real-time ticks, snapshots, and sequence numbers.

pages/6/05.s: See a complete protocol client perform Wesnoth's local handshake, read framed messages, and respond to one chat command.

pages/6/06.s: Understand how a local proxy relays two byte streams while preserving direction, framing, and the original messages.

pages/6/07.s: See how two processes communicate through named shared memory, with explicit layouts, permissions, synchronization, and cleanup.

pages/6/08.t: Named Pipes and Local Message Framing
pages/6/08.s: Compare byte and message modes in Windows named pipes, then account for framing, bounded reads, connection races, and handle ownership.

pages/6/09.s: Follow a player's command through Source's modules, prediction, server simulation, and snapshots, then connect those boundaries to settings and game files.

pages/9/01.s: See how saves, configuration, textures, maps, and archives preserve game state outside a running process, how a game turns an asset file into something it can draw or play, and how long that asset stays loaded, changes, or reloads.

pages/9/02.s: See how text saves encode state, how controlled comparisons reveal fields, and why writes must be atomic.

pages/9/09.s: Read offsets and bytes in a hex editor, decode a small binary save, compare two files, and update a checksum.

pages/9/03.s: Connect a visible game surface to its texture file, preserve the expected format, and package a reversible replacement, then read the same ideas in a 3D model (glTF) and a sound, including how a sound is placed between two ears and fades with distance.

pages/9/04.s: Understand how a game turns editable unit definitions into behavior and how small changes can be validated.

pages/9/05.s: Learn why archive entry names require path, size, and file-type checks before a mod is installed.

pages/9/06.s: Use a manifest to record installed files, hashes, and restore actions so a mod can be checked and removed.

pages/9/07.s: Separate byte integrity from publisher identity through hashes, signatures, certificates, and Windows trust checks.

pages/9/08.s: Compare encoding, hashing, MACs, and encryption, then follow the keys and metadata needed to protect a save.

pages/12/01.s: See why a game hosts Lua, run a small observer script, and learn the values and host boundary that later lessons build on.

pages/12/02.s: Lua's flexible tables and first-class functions express records, sequences, callbacks, methods, and lookup behavior.

pages/12/03.s: An embedded Lua VM can act only through the host functions and libraries the game exposes; typed contracts and error context keep that boundary clear.

pages/12/04.s: Immutable, versioned observations and bounded action requests connect Lua to game state without exposing arbitrary pointers.

pages/12/05.s: Named states, guarded transitions, timeouts, and a stop path make a scripted game observer predictable.

pages/12/06.s: Memory and instruction limits, tracebacks, and failure handling keep useful scripts from overrunning their host.

pages/1/12.s: Build a Turing machine by hand, see why one computer can run every program, and learn which questions about programs no tool can always answer.

pages/12/07.t: From Lua Source to a Tiny Virtual Machine
pages/12/07.s: Tokens, syntax, bytecode, and a bounded interpreter loop turn a short Lua-like expression into machine behavior.

pages/12/08.t: Values, Tables, Strings, and Garbage Collection
pages/12/08.s: See how a dynamic language represents values, why tables combine array and map behavior, and why automatic memory management must understand shared references and cycles.

pages/12/09.s: Understand VM call frames, multiple returns, captured locals, open and closed upvalues, and the host boundary where native functions enter Lua.

pages/10/01.t: The Running Game as a Process
pages/10/01.s: An executable becomes a process with threads, modules, handles, and Windows-managed state; the PEB and TEB reveal useful structure without being a safe API.

pages/10/09.s: Native code, Mono, IL2CPP, .NET, and Java expose different evidence about objects and their lifetimes; classify a build before trusting an offset.

pages/10/02.s: Learn why a version label is not enough and how a verified SHA-256 manifest ties addresses, patterns, mods, and patches to exact files.

pages/13/06.s: Object identity, field offsets, and layouts must be recovered for each build through several independent access patterns.

pages/10/03.s: A process ID names a target; tokens, integrity levels, DACLs, and access masks decide which operations Windows permits.

pages/10/04.s: Windows handles are capabilities with lifetimes. Rust ownership and RAII make leaks and double closes easier to prevent.

pages/10/05.t: Virtual Address Spaces and Page Protections
pages/10/05.s: Pages, regions, and R/W/X permissions explain why a game address can exist, fail, or change meaning.

pages/10/06.s: A game's threads share process resources while retaining separate execution contexts and call stacks; scheduling and races shape what an observer sees.

pages/10/07.t: From Win32 Calls to Kernel Services
pages/10/07.s: A Windows API call crosses layers of exports, native APIs, and system calls before a kernel service acts on a request.

pages/14/01.t: What an Operating System Kernel Does
pages/14/01.s: The processor separates user and kernel authority. System calls, scheduling, memory, interrupts, and drivers show what the kernel does for a running game.

pages/14/07.s: Privilege bits, page permissions, API stubs, handle checks, and NTSTATUS together explain one request's route through the kernel.

pages/10/08.s: A small dump preserves selected threads, modules, registers, and stacks for later inspection without a running process.

pages/11/01.s: A loaded module has a path, bytes, signer, and dependency context; names alone cannot prove which code entered a game.

pages/11/02.t: DLL Loading and the Loader Lock
pages/11/02.s: Mapping imports and running DllMain require careful ordering; a tiny entry point avoids work that can deadlock the loader.

pages/11/03.s: Runtime export lookup turns an optional Windows API into a checked capability with an explicit ABI and fallback.

pages/14/02.s: Drivers translate operating-system requests into hardware work through I/O packets, registers, interrupts, and DMA, including the path from key press to game input.

pages/14/08.s: Control-code fields, device registers, interrupt work, and USB reports reveal how a driver turns a request or key press into an observable result.

pages/11/05.s: Kernel drivers have authority beyond a game process; driver inventories and narrow privileges make that boundary visible.

pages/11/06.s: DMA gives devices a path to memory, while page tables and IOMMUs determine which physical bytes correspond to an address.

pages/11/07.s: An offline page-table walk maps one process address to bounded offsets in a RAM capture, including reads that cross pages.

pages/11/08.s: A plausible translation can still describe the wrong process, build, or moment; provenance and independent checks give offline bytes meaning.

pages/13/01.s: A game's state changes through transitions. Invariants describe which states remain valid, while controls and detectors answer different parts of that promise.

pages/13/07.t: Telemetry as Evidence of Game Behavior
pages/13/07.s: Bounded event traces connect inputs, decisions, and effects so a suspected control gap becomes a testable claim.

pages/13/02.s: An integrity check is meaningful only when its inputs, timing, and decision path cover the state it promises to protect.

pages/13/03.s: Anti-debug behavior is a sequence of signals, interpretations, and responses; explicit states expose false positives and weak assumptions.

pages/13/04.s: Reversible transforms can hide a value in memory without providing encryption; round trips and controlled changes reveal the rule.

pages/11/04.s: Three small defenses show how an apparently valid check can miss the path that produces an effect, and how to repair its invariant.

pages/13/08.s: Three toy game controls reveal a recurring mismatch between the checked proxy and the effect that actually changes state.

pages/13/09.s: Eight further failure modes, from wrapping arithmetic to partial commits, show where an invariant must be enforced.

pages/14/03.s: A hypervisor gives guest machines controlled access to processors and memory through VM exits, two-stage translation, and snapshots.

pages/14/09.s: A guest relies on virtualization support and two-stage address translation; walking one address shows both the isolation and its cost.

pages/14/12.s: Follow a microcontroller from reset to Rust, build a working firmware image, and understand what changes when you program a physical board.

pages/14/05.s: Consoles combine familiar computer parts with secure boot, signing, and platform rules that shape how games can run and be modified.

pages/14/04.s: JTAG began as a board-test port and became a hardware debugging path through scan chains, the TAP controller, and SWD.

pages/14/10.t: JTAG Scan Chains and Debug Access
pages/14/10.s: Shift registers, TAP states, IDCODE, and SWD packets show how a hardware debugger discovers and controls a chip.

pages/14/06.s: An emulator recreates a console in software through instruction execution, memory-mapped I/O, timing, graphics, audio, and save states.

pages/14/11.s: A toy console makes instruction costs, frame timing, save states, and register races concrete inside a Rust emulator.

pages/15/01.s: Separate a player's requests from the game's decisions, and connect prevention, detection, and fair enforcement.

pages/15/02.s: Validate commands against server-owned state, withhold hidden information, and use replays carefully.

pages/15/03.t: Server Plugins, Counters, and False Flags
pages/15/03.s: Read Macrodox and other SourceMod designs as measurement systems, separating button edges, weighted history, and enforcement.

pages/15/04.s: Connect local integrity checks and kernel protection to boot trust, driver risk, privacy, and reliability.

pages/15/05.s: Compare detector signals and count the real people behind a false-positive rate.

pages/15/06.s: Combine game, platform, league, and server observations without treating duplicated reports as independent proof.

pages/15/07.t: Cheat Categories from the Defender's Side
pages/15/07.s: Connect different locations of unauthorized code and automation to the observations and boundaries a defender can use.

pages/15/08.s: Compare documented protection boundaries and lifetimes without treating product names as proof of effectiveness.

pages/15/09.t: Designing a Game That Is Hard to Cheat In
pages/15/09.s: Place authority, disclosure, retries, evidence, and permissions into the game's design from the beginning.

1.s: Connect computer and game loops to programming, Rust, memory, and a first scan.

2.s: Connect a built program to assembly, breakpoints, stable addresses, and reversible detours.

3.s: Decode bytes into numbers, then recover typed values, objects, and collections across process boundaries.

4.s: Follow engine-owned state through snapshots, coordinates, decisions, feedback, and NPC behavior.

5.s: Read executable layout, then use scanning, disassembly, debugging, and traces to explain running code.

6.s: Build from DLL contracts to loading, hooks, input, commands, and reliable feature lifetimes.

7.s: Turn coordinates into camera views and pixels, then integrate rendering features and menus.

8.s: Follow messages from bytes and framing through protocol states, proxies, and local channels.

9.s: Read text and binary saves, assets, and mods as formats with integrity and trust constraints.

10.t: Lua, Host Boundaries, and Virtual Machines
10.s: Express behavior through Lua, then connect computation limits to bytecode, values, and call frames.

11.s: Connect build and object identity to access rights, memory, threads, kernel services, and dumps.

12.s: Trace DLL and driver boundaries before validating offline physical-memory captures.

13.s: Use invariants and telemetry to explain integrity checks, value transforms, control gaps, and repairs.

14.s: Connect guest execution and firmware to console architecture, hardware debugging, and software emulation.

15.s: Protect server authority and information, interpret detector errors, and combine client protection with fair review.
